Setting up of international airports in Madhya Pradesh  
 *81. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to 
state:  
(a)  the number of airports operating in Madhya Pradesh at present alongwith the loca-
tions thereof; 
(b)  whether any proposal is under consideration of Government for construction of new 
airports of international standard in order to extend facility for movement of the people of 
Madhya Pradesh as also to promote tourism; and 
(c)  if so, by when the construction work of these airports would be started? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRIPRAFUL 
ATEL): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a) to (c) Airports Authority of India (AAI) owns a nd manages four airports namely,  
hopal, Khajuraho, Indore and Jabalpur in Madhya Pra desh. AAI also manages a Civil  
inclave at Gwalior. The airports at Bhopal, Indore and Khajuraho have been taken up for  
ogradation/modernisation under the 35 Non-Metro airports modernisation project of AAI.  
odernisation work at the said three airports is scheduled for completion by mid 2009.

SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Sir, acquisition of land for international airports 
is a serious issue which the Civil Aviation Ministr y is facing. In Goa, when the issue of 
expansion of Dabolim airport came, the entire land is occupied by the Indian Navy. Sir. the 
land belongs to the Government of Goa. But, the Air ports Authority of India is asking for 
more land from the Indian Navy, not from the Government of Goa! This is indirectly recognising 
the right of the Indian Navy. Whereas, the records and title shows that land belogns to the 
Government of Goa. As a result, the Ministry had to spend a lot of time in getting land for 
expansion of airport. Sir, his Ministry should have  taken up the issue with the Minisry of 
Defence saying that they should give up their right  on land and should not claim that the 
land belongs to them so that land is easily made available for expansion of airport. Therefore, 
at this stage, I would like to know the status of the land that you have wrongly asked from the 
Defence Ministry rather than asking from the Goa Government.  
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, first and foremost, this does not pertain to the main question 
because we are talking about airports in Madhya Pradesh. However, since I have firsthand 
knowledge of this problem raised by the hon. Member, I will answer it. The Goa airport, per 
se, is airport of the Indian Navy, and we are only running a civil enclave there. Of course, we

have had many issues, from time to time, because Goa seriously requires a new airport. But, 
in the meantime, this airport needs to be upgraded because it attracts very high-end tourism. 
In fact, it attracts all categories of tourism. Goa  has become a very popular destination 
worldwide, as well as, within the country. I can as sure the hon. Member that there is no 
question of the Government of India or the Ministry of Civil Aviation talking to the wrong 
agencies for the purpose of land. We will, certainly, be talking to whoever is the owner of the 
land. In this case, we will be talking to the India n Navy, as well as, the Goa Government 
 in case of some additional land which is outside t he territory of the airport.  
SHRI SHANTA RAM LAXMAN NAIK: Even the encroachers are there.  
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: I cannot answer about encroachments. But, I can, certainly, tell 
you that in this case I have personally conducted m any meetings in my office with all 
agencies. I have met the Navy Chief. I have met the Defence Secretary. My officials have 
been holding meetings. I have met the concerned authorities in the Government of Goa on 
several occasions. Of course, this has gone a little bit round and round. I can, certainly, feel 
that there would be some resolution in the near future. I would also urge you to support us 
and take up this issue at the local level also and try to see that this land is made available. We 
are ready to build a very good terminal there. We have all the resources to do so. But, at the 
same time, in the absence of land, this issue is something which has not yet been resolved.

it has been revealed that out of 34 industries, in seven industries, the number of contract/ 
casual/contingency workers is more than the regular workers; in two industries, the number 
of contract labourers and that of regular labourers is almost equal, and in eight industries, the 
number of contract workers in the total workforce ranges between 30 per cent and more than 
50 per cent. If we see the public sector in general , we will find that in other Ministers th» 
situation is even more precarious which clearly ref lects that these contract/casual/corfSln-
gency workers are being utilised in the regular, pe rmanent and perennial operational jobs, 
which is not permissible under the law of the land. 
Sir, my first supplementary is: (a) In view of such a violation of the law of the land in the 
work places run by the Government of India, I would like to know whether the hon. Minister 
is going to instruct the concerned management and take direct initiative to see that the rule 
of law is established in the work places run by the Government of India itself, and ensure that 
the contract workers engaged in the regular operational areas are immediately regularised.

State Government, but the minimum wage applicable to that industry. If it is not done, again,

SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV: Mr. Chairman, Sir, it is very unfortunate that the hon. 
Member is saying that the Government of India is following illegal practices. No, I strongly 
condemn this idea of the hon. Member. He is a seaso ned and old Member of the House. 
When we make a tender in various parts of the country, we give our wages. We get them. We 
take some permanent labourers but, on the spot there, it is more reasonable and competitive 
for us to take local labourers; so, there is no illegality. But we maintain the minimum wage law 
of that particular State where they do the work. The minimum wage varies from State to State, 
the best being in Kerala. In other States, it is no t that good. I do agree that it needs to be 
considered by the Ministry of Labour and not by me. As regards his question as to whether 
we will permanently absorb these labourers; no, but we give them the facilities of Provident 
Fund and other.things. If they work for seven days. Provident Fund is cut from their salaries 
and is deposited. Sometimes, if they participate in he contributory system of Provident Fund, 
it is cut from their wages. This is one of the innovations in India. In other parts of the world 
wherever I have gone, I have found that Provident Fund is not given to the casual workers. 
So, we should feel proud that in our country the la bour laws are such as to protect the 
interests of the working class. I request the hon. Member not to form an idea that we are 
doing something illegal.

Oral Answers  [4 MARCH 2008]  to Questions   13  
Inflation rate in India  
†*84. DR.MURLlMANOHARJOSHJ:tt  
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA:  
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state:  
(b)  whether it is a fact that during the period from September, 2007 to January, 2008 the 
inflation rate in India has remained high in comparison to the other leading economies of the 
world; 
(c)  if so, the details thereof; 
(d)  what has been the average inflation rate during the  above said period in America 
England, European countries, Japan and China; and 
(e)  the extent to which this rate is more or less, in comparison to the average inflation rate 
of lndia? 
THE FINANCE MINISTER (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) A Statement is placed 
on the Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a) to (c) In India, rate of inflation, based on Consumer Price Index for industrial workers 
(CPI-I W) declined from 6.4 per cent in September-2007 to 5.5 per cent in January 2008. Rate of 
inflation in major advanced economies firmed up beginning September 2007. Amongst major 
economies, rate of inflation in January 2008, as measured by the consumer price index (CPI), 
was 4.3 per cent in the US, 2.2 per cent in the UK, 3.2 per cent in the Euro area as compared 
with 2.8 per cent, 1.8 per cent and 2.1 per cent, respectively, in September 2007. In Japan, 
inflation increased to 0.7 per cent in December 2007 from -0.2 per cent in September 2007 and 
in China to 7.1 per cent in January 2008 from 6.2 per cent in September 2007. The average 
inflation in India was 5.7 per cent for the period September 2007-January 2008. The average 
CPI inflation during the period September 2007-January 2008 for the US, the UK, Euro area, 
Japan (September 2007-December 2007) and China was 3.8 per cent, 2.1 per cent, 2.8 per cent, 
0.4 per cent and 6.6 per cent, respectively (Table I).  
(d) While the average inflation rate in other leading economies—US, UK, Euro area and Japan 
was less than in India, inflation rate in China at 6.6 per cent was higher than inflation in India.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the Reserve Bank of India put out its Annual Monetary 
Policy Statement which estimated that the inflation in the current year would be between 4.S 
per cent and 5 per cent and the effort was to contain it below 4.5 per cent. I have said that the 
effort is to contain it below 4.5 per cent and keep it closer to 4 per cent. I agree with the hon. 
Member. There is some pressure on the food prices a nd on a number of occasions I have 
explained tried to explain—why there is pressure on  food prices. There is a supply-demand 
mismatch in India. There are a number of factors th at affect the food prices. Firstly, the 
production has stagnated for several years. We had a supply-demand mismatch in wheat, 
rice and pulses for many years. So far as edible oi l and pulses are concerned, we always 
imported some pulses and edible oil. International prices have risen. As I said in my Budget 
Speech, and I said again that wheat prices have ris en by 88 per cent world-wide and rice 
prices by 15 per cent since April of this year. We have increased MSP for wheat and rice 
significantly over the last three years. Finally, the demand has also risen because of money 
supply having increased. Thanks to higher rate of i nvestment, Investment to GDP ratio is 
now over 36 per cent. So, all these factors together have put some pressure on prices. Now, 
what can the Government do and what will the Govern ment do? The Government will 
carefully watch the situation and take such monetary measures which are necessary. As the 
hon. Member knows, monetary measures have a flip si de. The interest rate will rise. 
Therefore, we have to balance between price stability and growth. The second measure that 
the Government must take is to reduce the supply-demand mismatch. It is the management of 
the supply side which is the most challenging task in this year, as well as. in 2008-09, and the 
Government has taken and will take measures to manage the supply side of food articles.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, hon. Member, in the last part of his question, asked a 
specific question, "How do we propose to remove the mismatch?" The National Food Secu-
rity Mission and the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana are designed to remove the mismatch. 
The goal is to increase rice production by 10 milli on tonnes, wheat production by eight 
million tonnes and pulses production by two milion tonnes. This is the most comprehensive 
programme that has been devised in the recent past to sharply step up total production of 
rice, wheat and pulses. We have allocated, as hon. Member knows, Rs. 25 thousand crores 
for one Mission and Rs. 4,882 crores for the other Mission. If we are able to step up produc-
tion, that will certainly help the supply side, and medium to long term answer is to augment 
the supply side of food articles.

DR. K. MALAISAMY: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. The  hon. Minister has already

control and contain the uncontrollable factors to moderate the inflation rate.  
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, there are some factors which are not in our control. For 
example, the price of crude oil is not in our control. Among commodities, the prices of a large 
number of metals are not under our control. As far as food prices are concerned, if India is 
nearly self-sufficient in wheat, rice, pulses, edible oil, we are largely insulated from world 
prices. But if we are dependent on imports, to that extent, we are subject to world prices.and 
to that extent, it is beyond our control. For example, edible oil. Edible oil price has increased 
by over 100 per cent from the exporting countries like Malaysia and Indonesia in the last few 
months, and we are dependent on importing edible oil. Similarly, pulses. We import pulses. 
Pulses are not available in many countries of the world and prices of pulses have also gone 
up. Therefore, to the extent that we are dependent on imports like crude oil, metals, edible oil 
and pulses, we are not insulated from world prices. What is it that is within our control? It is 
certainly within our control to increase production and productivity. Yield gap between State 
and State is so large. If we can get the yield out of a Bihar field equal to the yield a Punjab 
field, we will be nearly self-sufficient. Monetary policy is also withing our control. But, 
monetary policy is within the domain of the Reserve Bank of India and the Reserve Bank's 
stated goal, as is Government's goal, is to ensure growth with reasonable price stability.

going down?  
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM) (a) and (b) The Sensex moves 
up or down depending On the changing perceptions of investors — domestic and overseas, 
retail and institutional — about the economy, the s ector and the company. This perception is 
influenced by many factors including the macro-economic environment, the growth poten-
tial of the economy, policy credibility of the Government,corporate performance, domestic 
and international events and market sentiments. The  recent fall in the stock markets is 
arrributed among other factors, to the sub-prime mo rtgage crisis in the US, change in the 
monetary stanse of developed countries, the expecte d recession in US, firming up of oil 
prices, Yen carry trade, the policy measures on Offshore Derivative Instruments by SEBI, 
impact of primary market issues, relative valuations in emerging markets, etc.  
(a)  The loss or gain arising from market movements is notional. This arises continuously 
with change in the value of the portfolios of investors with changes in prices of constituent 
securities. However, the actual loss or gain no par ticular investors depends on the invest-
ment time horizon of those investors. While the Sensex declined by 7.4% on 21st January 
2008, it increased by 34.5% during this fiscal on a  point to point basis from end of 
March, 2007 to end of February, 2008. 
(b)  The authorities do not try to manage or control movement of stock indices. They have 
put in place systems and practices to promote a safe, transparent and efficient market and to 
protect market integrity. The systems instituted include advanced risk management mecha-
nisms comprising on-line monitoring and surveillanc e, various limits on position, margin 
requirements, circuit filters, etc. The systems and practices are reviewed continuously and 
modified to meet emerging needs. Measures taken to broaden and deepen markets include 
scree based trading system, dematerialization of se curities, corporatization and 
demutualization of exchanges, settlement through cl earing corporation, trading in of 
derivatives.etc. Besides, SEBI maintains a constant  vigil in the market,and incase of any 
abnormality, takes appropriate action against the concerned entities.

state:  
(a) whether it is a fact that according to the original financial documents presented to the 
Board, Air India had recorded its biggest ever net loss of Rs. 541.3 crore for the financial year

comfort has resulted in what a Board member described as 'a loss of customer confidence';

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRIPRAFUL 
PATEL): (a) The erstwhile Air India has incurred a net loss of Rs. 447.93 crores during the

have been taken by NACIL. These are expected to boost the profits of the company.

Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(c)  whether the production of oil and gas in the oil an d gas reserves found in Krishna 
Godavari basin, Tapti Gas area and Bikaner region of Rajasthan will be started in the year 
2008; 
(d)  if so, the total quantum of oil and gas to be made available from these areas; 
(e)  whether Government has prepared any new licensing policy for the exploration of oil 
and gas; and 
(f)  if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MURLI DEORA) (a) In 
Krishna Godavari basin, Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC) started commercial 
oil and gas production in October, 1998. In 2006-07, production by ONGC in onland areas of 
KG basin was about 602 tonnes per day of crude oil and 4 million metric standard cubic 
metres per day (MMSCMD) of natural gas. In July 2008, additional natural gas of 40 MMSCMD 
from Krinshna Godavari deepwater areas is likely to  be produed by Reliance Industries 
Limited and NIKO Resources Limited Joint Venture. 
In Rajasthan, ONGC and Oil India Limited are producing natural gas at the rate of 0.75 
MMSCMD. In second quarter of 2009, crude oil peak production of 6 million metric tonnes 
per annum is likely to be produced by Cairn Energy India Pvt. Ltd. 
12 MMSCMD of natural gas is produced from Tapti fie ld by British Gas Exploration 
Production India Limited (BGEPIL) 
(b) As on 1.4.2007,  KG basin, initially in place o il and gas reserves of 970.52 million 
metric tonnes of oil equivalent (MMTOE) have been e stablished. In Rajasthan, initially in 
place oil and gas reserves of 310.36 MMTOE have been established. In Tapti field, initially in 
place oil and gas reserves of 114.96 MMTOE have been established.

(c) and (d) Government of India approved the New Ex ploration and Licensing Policy 
(NELP) in 1997 and it became effective in February,  1999. Since then licenses for 
exploration are being awarded only through a compet itive bidding system and , National 
Oil Companeis (NOCs) are required to compete on an equal footing with Indian and 
foreign companies to secure Petroleum Exploration L icenses (PELs). Six rounds of bids 
have so far been concluded under NELP, in which pro duction sharing contracts for 162 
exploration blocks have been signed. Under NELP, 56  oil and gas discoveries in 17 blocks 
have already been made in Cambay onland, North East  Coast and Krishna-Godavari 
deepwater areas, for which, development plans by the operators are in progress.  
With Exploration and development efforts made under NELP, Natural Gas production in 
the country is likely to be doubled by end of Eleventh Five Year Plan from the present level 
of gas productin of about 90 million standard cubic metres per day (MMSCMD).  
Under seventh round of NELP which was launched on 1 3th December, 2007, 
Government is offering 57 exploration blocks. The offered blocks include — 19 deepwater 
blocks, 9 shallow water blocks and 29 onland blocks . Exploration blocks in onland areas 
are located in the States of Assam (1), Bihar (3), Chhattisgarh (1), Gujarat (11), Madhya 
Pradesh (2), Rajasthan (3), Tamil Nadu (2) and West Bengal (6). Out of 19 deepwater blocks, 
15 exploration blocks are in western offshore areas and 3 exploration blocks are in eastern 
offshore areas. One deepwater exploration blocks is in Andaman Nicobar basin. Amongst 
shallow water blocks, 6 blocks are in Mumbai basin in western offshore, while 3 blocks are 
in KG basin in eastern offshore.  
Amendments to the Income Tax Act, 1961 
 *88 . SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY: Will the Minsiter of FINANCE be pleased to state:  
whether Government propose to bring out the necessa ry amendments to Section 10 (17) of 
the Income TaxAct, 1961 providing exemption of tax on all allowances to Members of 
Legislative Assembly of Andhra Pradesh at par with the Members of Parliament; 
if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; 
whether any representation in this respect has been  received from the State Government of 
Andhra Pradesh; and 
if so, what action has been taken thereon by the Central Government? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) Clause (17) of 
Section 10 of the Income Tax Act exempts from income tax specified allowances received by 
any person by reason of his membership of Parliament or of any State Legislature. Prior to 
1.4.2007, in the case of MPs, the following allowances were exempt under section ,10(17) of 
the Income Tax Act, 1961:  
(0 DailyAllowance;  
(ii) Constituency Allowance.  
In contrast, in the case of MLAs, the following allowances were exempt:  
(0 DailyAllowance;  
(ii) All other allowances up to an aggregate limit of Rs. 2000/- p.m.  

26    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Starred Questions  
In order to bring parity in tax treatment of allowa nces received by_MPs and MLAs, 
Section 10(17) was amended vide Finance Act, 2006 with effect from 1.4.2007. After the 
amendment, as in the case of MPs, the following allowances of MLAs are also exempt—  
(0 Daily Allowance; and  
(ii) Constituency Allowance, irrespective of any limit.  
All other allowances of MPs as well as MLAs are taxable. In view of the above, the tax 
treatment of allowances received by MPs and MLAs has become uniform.  
Given the existing parity, granting further exempti on to any other allowances received 
by MLAs of Andhra Pradesh may not be desirable. A r epresentation dated 09.08.2007 
was received on this issue from the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh. A reply dated 
13.09.2008 was sent to the Chief Minister of Andhra  Pradesh clarifying the issue raised 
by him.

Archaeological Survey of India has set up an air pollution laboratory at Taj Mahal, Agra

The clay pack method is used for the scientific cle aning of marble surface in order to 
safely and effectively remove superficial accretion s. It has been planned to take up the 
task of mud pack cleaning treatment in two phases. In the first phase of work, the arches 
including the marble screens and platform terrace walls of the monuments facing Yamuna 
has already been initiated and expected to be completed by second week of June, 2008 with

The treatment of marble surface of the Taj Mahal employing clay pack/mud pack treat-
ment technique has been adopted since 1983-84. This technique is an internationally recog-
nized method based on absorption principle. Fuller's Earth activated with certain suitable 
chemicals is used for this purpose. The marble surf ace to be cleaned is covered with a 
two millimeter thick layer of the paste of Fuller's Earth prepared in distilled water. The mud 
pack is covered with polythene sheets in order to a llow sufficient time for action. When 
the paste dries naturally, it is removed from the s urface with soft nylon brushes and the 
treated surface is washed with distilled water. The  accretions are absorbed by the paste, 
leaving the stone surface clean. This method is non -absorbed by the paste, leaving the 
stone surface clean. This method is non-abrasive, non-corrosive and quite effective in the 
removal of adherent accretionary deposits.  
References are available about the advisability and  safety of using poulticing 
materials for marble cleaning. This method has been successfully used in U.K. and Itlay.

However, a number of steps have been taken to reduce incidents of frauds in banks. Reserve 
Bank of India, as a part of its supervisory process, has been sensitizing banks from time to 
time about common fraud prone areas, modus operandi and the measures to be taken by 
them to prevent/reduce the incidents of frauds in banks. RBI has issued guidelines to banks 
on credit operations which were consolidated in a master Circular dated 2.7.2007. In terms of 
this Circular, banks should independently assess the credit risk while issuing credit cards to 
customers. While issuing the cards, the terms and conditions for issue and usage of a credit 
card should be mentioned in clear and simple language (preferably in English, Hindi and local 
language) comprehensible to the credit card user. As per the master Circular, the most impor-
tant terms and conditions (termed as 'standard set of conditions') should be highlighted and 
advertised/sent separately to the prospective customer at all stages i.e. during marketing, at the 
time of application, at the acceptance stage and in important subsequent communications.  
RBI has also taken various measures to prevent bank frauds and in particular has advised 
bank to introduce a system of concurrent audit cove ring branches accounting for 50% of 
their business (Deposit & Advances), prescribed detailed Know Your Customer (KYC) norms, 
advised banks to constitute a Special Committee of the Board for exclusive monitoring of 
large value frauds of Rs. One crore and above and t o set up Fraud Prevention Committee/ 
Task Forces. RBI has further advised the banks to f ollow due diligence in their Human 
Resource Policy and Accounting systems and procedur es with a view to prevent frauds.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI-PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL ): (a) to (b) The Advisory Committee on Flow of Credit to Agriculture and Related 
Activities from the Banking System set up by the Reserve Bank of India under Chairmanship of Prof. 
V.S. Vyas had examined various issues relating to agriculture credit and submitted its final report 
on June 30,2004.  
Several recommendations of the Vyas Committee have been accepted and communicated to the 
Banks for implementation. These, inter-alia, include: (i) waiver of margin/security norms for 
agricultural loans upto Rs. 50,000/-, and in case of loans for agri-clinics and agribusinesses upto Rs. 
5 lakh; (ii) bringing about procedural simplifications; and (iii) financing of oral lessees and landless 
agricultural labourers throught he Self Help Group and joint Liability Group approach.  
Considerable progress has been achieved in some part of the region in devising the land 
documents with adequate legal backing for collateral to loans such as:- 
(i) Mizoram has a system of issuing Land Settlement  Certificate (LSC) conferring 
transferable ownership rights over land holdings.  
(ii) This system is followed in two hill districts of Assam and community lands have also 
been leased on long term basis to private companies.  
(iii) The practice of issuing Land Possession Certificate (LPC) is in vogue in Arunachal 
Pradesh.  
(iv) In Nagaland, except in Sema and Konyak areas, land is owned by individuals. With 
the amendment of Section 162 of the Assam Land and Revenue Regulations, 1886 in 
2002, the land can now be mortgaged in favour of any nationalised bank and PSU, 
provided the transfer of land is made only to indigenous inhabitants of Nagaland.  
(v) No land in Tripura is owned by the community, e ither they are in possession of 
land owners (patta holders) or in possession of For est Department (State 
Government). While the land under patta holders can be transferred to others, for the 
jhum cultivation in forest, it is possible to issue certificate of land holding by Sub-
Divisional Magistrate/Block Development Officer.  
(vi) In Meghalaya though legislature had enacted provision for creation of charge on land 
and mortgage of the same for taking bank loan way back in 1976, its progress remained 
hindered due to lack of creation of formal land ownership/possession documents.  
(vii) In Manipur, only very few pockets of hill areas have been surveyed and pattas have 
been issued by government on which mortgages can be created. In the rest of the hill 
areas issue of LPC has not yet taken place.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN 
KUMAR BANSAL ) (a) and (d) As on 31 st March, 2007, the Gross Non-Performing Assets 
(NPAs) of Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) stood a t Rs. 50,552 crore. A statement 
indicating bank-wise details of Gross NPAs of SCBs is given in the Statement. (See below)  
The factors responsible for NPAs, inter-alia, include diversion of funds by the borrower and 
wilful default in repayment, deficiency in credit a ppraisal and supervision, inefficient 
management of the unit financed, poor follow up and monitoring, unviability or sickness of 
the unit due to change in technology demand pattern and other policy etc., non-completion

materials etc., labour problems,natural calamities, delay in disposal by courts of suits filed by 
banks, etc. However, the banks monitor their loan a ccounts at various levels and take 
appropriate corrective action, on an ongoing basis, to arrest slippages to NPA category. 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Government of I ndia have taken various steps to 
improve assets quality of the banks which, inter-alia, include prescribing prudential 
norms for provisioning and classification of non-pe rforming assets, guidelines for 
prevention of slippages, introduction of Corporate Debt Restructuring mechanism. One 
Time Settlement schemes, enactment of (i) The Secur itisation and Reconstruction of 
Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Intere st (SARFAESI) Act, 2002, (ii) the 
Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005, and (iii) the Recovery of Debts due 
to Banks and Financial Institutions (DRT) Act, 1993, etc. Due to concerted efforts, the net 
NPAs of the SCBs have declined from 4.4% of Net Adv ances as on 31st March, 2003 to

Recovery of outstanding loans by PSU Banks  
525. DR. V. MAITREYAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state:  
the total outstanding loans under various categories which are due for more than three years 
in various Public-Sector Banks; 
the reasons for the huge outstanding; 
the steps being taken to recover these loans; 
whether it is a fact that many banks are writing of f these loans as bad debts causing huge 
losses to the banks vis-a-vis their performances; and 
if so, the reasons for writing off these loans? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRIP AWAN 
KUMAR BANSAL ): (a) As on 31.03.2007, public sector banks (PSBs)  had gross Non-
performing Assets (NPAs) amounting to Rs. 38,974 cr ore, out of which Rs. 14,275 crore 
were in Substandard Assets Category, Rs. 19,873 crore in Doubtful Assets Category and Rs. 
4,826 crore in Loss Assets Category. In percentage terms, these constituted 2.7% (gross 
NPAs), 1.0% (Sub-standard Assets), 1.4% (Doubtful A ssets) and 0.3% (Loss Assets) of 
the total advances of these banks.  
(b) and (c) The factors responsible for NPAs, inter-alia, include diversion of funds by the 
borrower and wilful default in repayment, deficienc y in credit appraisal and supervision, 
inefficient management of the unit financed, poor follow up and monitoring, unviability or 
sickness of the unit due to change in technology demand pattern and other policy etc.m non-
completion of project due to cost and time overruns and other factors, such as non-availability 
of raw materials etc., labour problems, natural cal amities, delay in disposal by courts of 
suits filed by banks, etc. However, the banks monitor their loan accounts at various levels 
and take appropriate corrective action, on an ongoi ng basis, to arrest slippages to NPA 
category.  
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Government of I ndia have taken various steps to 
improve asset quality of the banks which, inter-alia, include prescribing prudential norms 
for provisioning and classification of non-performi ng assets, guidelines for prevention of 
slippages, introduction of Corporate Debt Restructuring mechanism, One Time Settlement 
schemes, enactment of (i) The Securitisation and Re construction of Financial Assets and 
Enforcement of Security Interest (SARFAESI) Act, 2002, (ii) the Credit Information Compa-
nies (Regulation) Act, 2005, and (iii) the Recovery  of Debts due to Banks and Financial 
Institutions (DRT) Act, 1993, etc. Due to concerted efforts, the net NPAs of the PSBs have 
reduced from 4.5% of Net Advances as on 31 st March, 2003 to 1.1 % as on 31 st March, 2007.  
(d)and(e) The banks write-off NPAs for several reasons viz. to cleanse their balance sheets 
through prudential write-offs, to improve asset quality and to get rid of unrealisable portion of 
their bad loans in accordance with their Board approved policies and RBI  guidelines.

management mechanisms comprising on-line monitoring and surveillance, various limits on

ously reviewed continuously and modified to meet em erging needs. Measures taken to

Disincentives for checking external commercial borrowings  
551. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY : Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state:  
whether it is a fact that Government's disincentive s to check unbridled external 
commercial borrowings have not borne fruit; 
if so, the details thereof and reasons therefor; and 
the future action plan of Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN 
KUMAR BANSAL ): (a) to (c) The ECB Policy is reviewed continuous ly by the 
Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India, keeping in line with the 
evolving macro-economic situation, changing market conditions, sectoral 
requirements, developments in the external sector and the lessons of experience. With 
sovereign credit ratings of India enhanced to investment grade, the all-in-cost ceilings 
for ECB have been modified effective May 21, 2007. Further use of ECB proceeds for 
development of integrated township has since been withdrwan effective May 21,2007. 
Based on further review, the inflows of captial have been modulated through External 
Commercial Borrowings (ECB) by modifying some aspects of the policy with effect 
from August 7,2007, i.e. ECB up to USD 500 million per borrower company per 
financial year has been permitted only for foreign currency expenditure on import of 
capital goods and/or overseas acquisition and for permissible end-uses of ECB both 
under the Automatic and Approval Route. Borrowers proposing to svail of ECB up to 
USD 20 million for rupee expenditure for permissible end-uses would require prior 
approval of the Reserve Bank under Approval Route.  
Notwithstanding the above, the total ECBs registered with RBI amounts to USD 19.2 bn 
during April-October, 2007 as compared to US$ 11.8 bn during April-October, 2006 and US$ 
25.4 bn in fianncial year 2006-07. Thus it may be observed that in the absence of the above 
measures, the ECBs registered with RBI would have been much higher.

In market environment, the price discovered is the appropriate price at that moment under

Will the Minister of  PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS  be pleased to state:  
whether India is set to become world's third largest oil importer after USA and China before

whether India is ranked fourth in terms of oil impo rts, according to the World Energy 
Outlook 2007 report, in which rapid economic development in China and India would push

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL ): (a) to (c) As per the Executive Summary 
of report of IEF titled "World Energy Outlook 2007 : China and India Insights", before 
2025, India will overtake Japan to become the world 's third largest net importer of oil 
after United States and China. Yet, India's importa nce as a major exporter of refined oil 
products will also grow, assuming the necessary inv estments are forthcoming. Although 
recent discoveries are expected to boost gas produc tion, it is projected to peak between 
2020 and 2030 and then fall back. A growing share o f India's gas needs would therefore 
be met by imports entirely in the form of Liquefied  Natural Gas. The Executive summary, 
inter-alia, mentions following important points:  
(0 Economic development in China and India inevitably will push the global energy 
demand but it will also bring major economic benefits to the rest of the world.  
(ii) The world's primary energy needs are projected to grow by 55% between 2005 and 
2030 at an average annual rate of 1.8%  
(iii) Regarding energy security, the report stated that the rising global energy demand 
poses real and growing threat to world's energy sec urity. India's and China's 
growing participation in international trades heigh tens the importance of their 
collective efforts to enhance global energy security. How China and India re-

spond to the rising threats to their energy security will also affect rest of the 
world. Both countries are already taking action.  
(d) Various measures are being taken on a continuou s basis to reduce the country's 
dependence on the oil imports, which are as follows:  
(0 Carving out more and more areas for exploration for offer under various rounds of 
New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP)  
(ii) Quicker development of discovered reserves for enabling commencement of pro-
duction.  
(iii) Use of stimulation techniques for increasing production from existing fields.  
(iv) Application of Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR)/ Improved Oil Recovery (IOR) tech-
niques for increasing recovery factor from existing fields.  
(v) Arresting decline from ageing fields.  
(vi) Substitution of oil through use of non-convent ional source of energy such as 
bio-diesel, ethanol, etc.  
(vii) Construction of Strategic Storage of curde oil of 5 MMT capacity at three loca-
tions viz. Visakhapatnam, Mangalore and Padur, for meeting unf oreseen situa-
tions arising out of short term supply disruptions, natural calamities, etc.

Alternate source of fuel  
590. DR. V. MAITREYAN:  Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS  
be pleased to state:  
whether it is a fact that petroleum products are a huge source of drainage of foreign 
exchange as well as severe polluting agent in the country; 
if so, what steps are being taken to identify alter nate source of non-polluting fuel for the 
vehicles in the country; 
whether Government has intensified the R&D work in this area; and 
if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURALGAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL ): (a) In 2006-07, net expenditure of foreign 
exchange equivalent to US$ 39.6 billion was made in trade of petroleum products. During this 
period, US$ 48.4 billion were spent on the import of crude oil.  
(b) to (d) As efforts to suplement the consumption of petroleum products particularly for 
vehicular application and also to curb emissions, r esearch has been carried out by the 
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) to expl ore the possibility of utilizing 
alternatives for supplementing petrol and diesel. B io-fuels namely, bio-ethanol and bio-
diesel, hydrogen energy and battery operated vehicl es have been identified as potential 
future alternatives to supplement petrol and diesel.  
In the area of Bio-fuels, Ethanol-Gasoline fuels having 5% ethanol content is being used 
in 20 States and 4 Union Territories. Government ha s plans to introduce 10% ethanol in 
States where 5% ethanol is already being used. But vehicle manufacturers are asking for 
more time so as to study the effects of ethanol on material compatibility of in use vehicles.  
 

Written Answers to  [4 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions    131  
IOC R&D and SIAM have been advised to study the effect of 10% ethanol in gasoline on 
various type of in use vehicles.  
Besides spearheading commercialization of ethanol-blended gasoline in the country, Indian 
Oil has been in the fore front of technology develo pment for bio-diesel production from 
various edible/non-edible oils and its application in vehicles.  
Studies by Indian Oil's R&D Centre have established  that bio-diesel produced from 
Jatropha seeds was at par with bio-diesel produced from vegetable oils. In the past few 
years, the Indian Oil R&D Centre has studied the en tire value chain of bio-diesel, starting 
from Jatropha plantation to field trials on passeng er cars, light commercial vehicles and 
railway locos in collaboration with several vehicle manafucturers, Railways and State transpert 
undertakings.  
Homogenous Catalysed Single pot process has also be en developed for production of 
bio-diesel.  
India's first experimental hydrogen-CNG dispensing station was commissioned in the 
campus of IOC R&D at Faridabad and demonstration pr ojects are underway on use of 
Hydrogen-CNG blends in heavy and light vehicles. These projects are funded by Ministry of 
Petroleum and Natural Gas and National Hydrogen Energy Board (NHEB) under Ministry of 
New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) of the Government o f India.  
NHEB under MNRE has estimated about one million veh icles using pure hydrogen or 
hydrogen CNG blended fuel by 2020.  
Consequencies of price hike in petroleum product  
591 . SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI : Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS  
be pleased to state:  
whether Government has taken a decision to hike the  prices of petrol, kerosene, diesel and 
cooking gas recently; 
if so, the details of the price hike; 
how far such a hike shall have an adverse effect on the common man; and 
(d) the action expected to be taken by Government to treat this hike in price as a "Final 
* Hike" for this decade?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL ): (a) to (d) The global prices of crude oil and pe troleum 
products have remained high and volatile since 2004. In view of this, the Public Sector Oil 
Marketing Companies (OMCs) are incurring under-recoveries on domestic sale of sensitive 
petroleum products namely petrol, diesel, PDS kerosene and domestic LPG As passing on 
the entire impact of the steep increase in the oil prices to the consumers would have 
resulted in hardship to the common man, the retail selling prices of petrol, diesel, PDS 
Kerosene and domestic LPG have not been increased i n tandem with the international oil 
prices.  
To meet the escalation in international oil prices, the Government has adopted the principle 
of'equitable burden-sharing' between the Government, the oil PSUs and consumers to protect 
the interests of the common man, vulnerable sections of society and also the financial health 
of OMCs. In this context, the Government has made a marginal increase in petrol and diesel

prices by Rs. 2/litre and Re. 1 /litre respectively with effect from 15.2.2008 which is actually in 
the nature of a restoration of retail prices of the se products of their price level operating 
before February, 2007. The Government has issued Oil Bonds and Upstream Oil Companies 
have also contributed by offering discounts on crude oil and petroleum products to partially 
compensate the under-recoverie3 of OMCs.  
Despite the steep increases in international oil prices, the Government has not increased 
the prices of PDS kerosene during the last six years and of Domestic LPG during the last three 
years.  
The prices of crude oil and petroleum products in the international market fluctuates on 
daily basis Government is closely monitoring the international oil prices and will continue to 
protect the interests of consumers.  
Risk to oil pipeline in Jharia, Jharkhand  
592.  SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN : Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURA.LGAS  be pleased to state:  
whether the fire in the coal belt beneath Jharia town has become potential danger for the oil 
pipelines passing through that area; 
if so, the details thereof; 
how many pipelines are passing through that area and how many pipelines face risk; and 
what efforts have been made by Government to save those pipelines from caving in? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL ): (a) to (d) Based on the information made available by 
the oil Public Sector Undertakings, there is no oil pipeline passing through the coal belt of 
Jharia.  
However, Indian Oil Corporation Limited's (IOCL's) Haldia-Barauni Product Pipeline (HBPL), 
originating from Haldia (West Bengal) and terminating at Barauni (Bihar) passes through 
Raniganj (West Bengal), Rajbandh (Durgapur, West Be ngal), Asansol (West Bengal), 
Madhupur (Jharkhand), Jasidih (Jharkhand), Jhajha (Bihar) and Mokamah (Bihar). A 42-km. 
section of this pipeline passes through the coal belt area of Raniganj in West Bengal and this 
pipeline transverse along a route about 70km. away from Jharia.  
IOCL's HBPL is safe and close monitoring of coal mine fire is maintained to avoid any 
untoward incident..Physical patrolling of the pipel ine route is done regularly and a close 
watch is kept for any abnormal indications. Geological Survey of India and Indian Institute of 
Rock Mechanics have also been approached to get further information about coal belt area 
through which a section of HBPL is passing. Besides  these, close interaction is also being 
done with Eastern Coal Field Limited to obtain the latest information about these areas.

†611. SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS be pleased to state:  
whether India has tweaked the oil diplomacy agenda and plans to offer African nations a 
development package to help their economies and in return, India wants participating interests 
in the continent's proven oil and gas blocks, besides a commitment for long term oil and gas 
supplies; 
if so, whether Government will offer the package which includes setting up infrastructure projects 
in power, refining, steel and railways network; and 
(c) if so, whether these issues would be discussed in the forthcoming Indo-African 
conference?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL): (a) to (c) Keeping in view the desire of both India and the 
African nations to intensify and widen cooperation in the hydrocarbon sector, First-ever 
India Africa Hydrocarbon Conference and Exhibition was held in New Delhi on 6-7th

Statement  
STAND OF MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS :- 
[I]. That the Prior approval of the M/o Environment & Forests [Central Government] is 
required under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 to carry out any non-forestry activity on 
forest land (including the area as per the widened meaning given to word 'forest' by this 
Hon'ble Court in order dated 12.12.1996 in WP(C) No. 202 of 1995 in so far as applicability of 
the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 is concerned).  

156    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
[II]. That this Hon'ble Court, vide order dated 14.02.2000 in Writ Petition (C) No. 202 of 
1995, has banned any non-forestry activity within any National Park/Sanctuary, hence, if the 
area on which non-forestry activity is to be carried out falls within any National Park/Sanctuary, 
prior approval of this Hon'ble Court and the National Board for Wildlife is required before the 
proposal can be considered by the Central Government under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 
1980.  
[III]. According to the Guidelines issued under the  Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, 
which is contained in para 4.4 of the Handbook of Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 issued by 
the Ministry by Ministry of Environment & Forests, some projects involve use of forest 
Land as well as non-forest land. The State Government/project authorities sometimes start 
work on non-forest lands in anticipation of the app roval of the Central Government for 
release of the forest lands required for the projec ts. Though the provisions of the Act may 
not have technically been violated by starting of w ork on non-forest lands, expenditure 
incurred on works on non-forest lands may prove to be infructuous if diversion of forest land 
involved is not approved. Hence, if a project involves forest as well as non-forest land, work 
should not be started on non-forest land till approval of the Central Government for release 
of forest land under the Forest (Consevation) Act, 1980 has been given'.  
STAND OF PLANNING COMMISSION , WATER RESOURCES DIVISION :- 
"Planning Commission guidelines for according investment clearance (Dated 30.11.2000) 
clearly stipulates that" any project which is located in an Inter State river or its tributary will 
be deemed to involve interstate remification and as  such need investment clearance from 
Planning Commission". The Planning Commission's guidelines requiring clearance for change 
of water use pattern in an inter-state river or its tributary is subject to technical appraisal by 
a competent agency such a Central Water Commission. If the Planning Commission's guideline 
is now deemed to apply only for projects where Plan funds (Centre or State) are being used, 
then the guidelines can be circumvented by saying t hat the funds used will be non-Plan. 
This interpretation is too flexible. The spirit of the guidelines is that Inter-State water use 
pattern cannot be changed without approval irrespec tive of whether Plan or Non-Plan 
resources are used.

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   175  
SHRI R.K. DHAWAN (Bihar): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, with your permission, I rise to 
support the Motion of Thanks to the hon. President's Address. Sir, at the outset, I would like 
to thank the hon. President for her illuminating ad dress to Parliament. Sir, as this august 
House knows, the President's Address is a statement made on behalf of the Government; the 
Address represents, generally, the programmes and policies of the Government. It is not a 
catalogue of what all the Government has done. It i s a concise statement in the restrained 
language which gives the details, because it is not  possible to give all the details that the 
Government wishes to give, if I may say so. My colleague Janardhan Dwivediji has made a 
very lucid analysis of the programmes and policies of the Government and Shri Singhviji has 
quoted various figures. I would not like to take the time of the hon. House in repeating all 
that. However, I would like to say a few words on some subjects, primarily on agriculture.  
Sir, the Congress Party fought the 2004 elections on the philosophy that the objective of 
any Government is not the glory of the rulers but the happiness of the common man. I have 
no hesitation in saying, much to the discomfort of my friends in the Opposition, that this has 
been the major factor for the Government in framing policies and programmes, to be responsible 
and transparent on all counts, and the Government has achieved many strides.  
Last year, while speaking on the same Motion, I emphasised the importance of having a 
second Green Revolution. Sir, it is a matter of great exhilaration for me that the Government 
during the last one year has made tremendous progre ss towards attainment of this 
indispensable national objective. Sir, it is hearte ning to note from the Address that the 
National Food Security Mission has been set up to e nhance the production of rice, wheat 
and pulses by 10, 8 and 2 million tonnes during the  Eleventh Plan period. Sir, another 
praiseworthy action taken by the Government is Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana with an outlay 
of Rs.25,000 crores for farmers revival by setting up agriculture growth of 4 per cent in the 
Eleventh Plan by providing incentives to States. Sir, for understanding the need of Second 
Green Revolution to which our Bhandaryji also referred, one has to go back into the history 
of development of agriculture since Independence. Sir, when this country became independent, 
Shri Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister, had the vision and foresight that India had to 
catch up with the rest of the world in the field of  industrial development and without 
industrialisation economic growth will not be able to match the world. With that in mind, he 
set up public sector undertakings to have industrial infrastructure and took initiative for the 
private sector to grow. Sir, but for historical experiences India had gone through, it was not 
possible to regulate, it was not possible to allow private sector to have the growth in its own 
manner because of the limitation of resources at th at time, much investment could not be 
made in the agricultural sector and result was the country in the sixties' had to face a very 
difficult situation so far as wheat was concerned a nd had to depend on import of wheat to 
save the millions of people from starvation. Sir, w hen Mrs. Gandhi took over the reins of 
office, and I am a witness to those events from 1966 onwards, she felt that economic progress 
would be an illusion only until and unless we becom e self-sufficient in the production of 
food and agricultural products. So, this was the vi sion that Mrs. Gandhi took and the 
initiative she took to have the Green Revolution and the manner in which production grew in 
few years, India got self-sufficiency in food is ma tter of record that is for nobody else to 
dispute. Sir, I have got no doubt in my mind that the gigantic step that the Government has 
taken in the field of agriculture will be the harbinger of Second Green Revolution in India. Sir, 

176 Motion of Thanks  [RAJYA SABHA]  on President's Address  
the country has made tremendous economic progress, economic growth has been the 
phenomenon. But unless fruit and benefits of this economic growth reach the millions of people 
who toil and sweat in the fields to serve the country, it will be only a matter of speech. So, something 
has to be done about that to improve the lot of the farmers for which this UPA Government is totally 
committed. Sir, I feel gratified to the UPA Government that it is fully alive to the problems, needs, 
and predicaments of the farmers. It is no ordinary achievement that the Government has effected an 
unprecedented growth, steep hike of 50 per cent in the Minimum Support Price of wheat and 33 per 
cent for paddy in the last four years. There is no denying the fact that for better marketing facilities, 
more productive seeds, fertilisers, remunerative prices will all go a long way in solving the 
problems of the farmers. Sir, relief, which has been given to farmers who were groaning under 
burden for non-payment of debts because of their meagre income, could not be more timely. Sir, 
revolution budgetary help to the Indian farmers, inspired by the vision of Shrimati Sonia Gandhi, 
has been in the finest traditions of Nehru-Gandhi family and its total sense of commitment to that. 
Sir, as probably the House will remember, or, history is a witness to it, it was Shri Jawaharlal 
Nehru who dragged endless miles on foot in this scorching sun across the parched villages 
of Uttar Pradesh to share the suffering and hardships of the farmers and imbibe in them a spirit of 
oneness. It was Shri Jawaharlal Nehru who wrote in his Will that when he dies his ashes should be 
flown up and scattered in the fields where Indian farmers toiled. Sir, Indian farmers have always been 
the most endeared and revered entity of Indian nationhood for the Nehru-Gandhi family. Sir, it 
is the same shared feeling of oneness of Shrimati Sonia Gandhi with the Indian farmers and her 
total identification with the lot that has come to their rescue who were being weighed down by an 
unbearable burden of debt and blighted all their hopes, distress and suffering life. Sir, it is her total 
commitment to bring solace to those farmers and their families which has led to the unprecedented 
step in coming to their help and bringing new cheers to their life. In stretching the warm hand of 
help to them in their hour of agony, Shrimati Sonia Gandhi has exhibited the spirit of oneness with 
the Indian farmers in the sublime traditions of Nehru-Gandhi family. Sir, I have got no doubt in my 
mind that for years to come, this gesture which has been made to the farmers of India will be 
remembered as one of the greatest testimonies to the commitments of Shrimati Sonia Gandhi to 
welfare of the poor and the downtrodden of this country.

DR. P.CALEXANDER (Maharashtra): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I thank you for giving me 
an opportunity to participate in the discussions on the Motion of Thanks to the President's 
Address. I am conscious of the fact that this is the last opportunity for me to participate in a 
discussion the President's Address because in a ver y short time I will be completing my 
tenure in this House.  
I mention this because I wfeuld like to raise a few basic issues regarding the functioning of 
our democracy and share with you some of my concern s about the directions that our 
democracy has taken in recent years. I will be basing my speech mainly on the observations 
made by the President in her speech on three points . And my fourth point will be on a 
conspicuous omission that I wish to point out in the President's Speech.  
My first point, Sir, is concerning the last paragraph of the President's Speech which gives 
a ringing exhortation to the people of this country about the functioning of democracy in our 
country. I quote this sentence. It is a very inspiring sentence. It says, "Therefore, what you 
say and do in these hallowed portals of democracy will have a bearing not just on the destiny 
of our people, but also on the future of democracy and free societies around the world."  
Sir, the question that I wish to raise before the h on. House is this. Is this assumption 
about the health of our democracy really justifiable? We are implementing the parliamentary 
system of democracy for the last 60 years. The foundations for this system were truly laid by 
the greatest democrat of that time, not the greates t democrat of India, but the greatest 
democrat of that time, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru. By the time he finished his 18 years of 
stewardship of the State, people had begun to feel confident that our democracy was on 
proper lines. But if we now look at the direction our democracy has taken and the manner in 
which it is functioning in our country, I feel genuinely concerned whether we will last as a 
democracy for a long time. The basic principle of Parliamentary democracy is that it has to be 
founded on a sound and healthy party system. Some o ther systems of Government can be 
practised without reference to political parties, b ut the Parliamentary system can function 
only if you have a good, healthy and sound party system in the country. Let us ask ourselves 
this question honestly. Do we have a good party system in this country? At any rate taking 
into account the manner in which parties are functi oning today, can we call that really 
healthy? Or, have we distorted the basic concepts o f democracy in the working of our 
parties? How can we think of having a healthy democracy at the Government level, if at the 
party level we do not practise democracy? It is unt hinkable because it is a contradiction to 
have democracy being implemented by political parti es which do not practise democracy 
within the parties. I am concerned, Sir, at the trend that has set in today, by which parties are 
run without any elections. The people seem to have forgotten that the functionaries of the 
parties have to be elected according to the will of the party members. But we have converted 
elections into nominations. And, the culture that is prevailing in most political parties, with 
the exception of three, or, four, which I do not want to name today, is the nomination culture 
masquerading as elections. It is all settled somewhere as to who is to be the President of the 
State party, who is to be the convenor of this, or,  the chairman of that, and, then, there are 
supposed to have been approved by the people through elections. This will eat into the  

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   203  
vitals of the political system in our country. After some time, a whole generation will grow up 
thinking that this is how party system should be do ne, and, then, our democracy will get 
completely devalued. Sir, this is a warning signal that I am raising, after deep study and full 
sense of responsibility. When the Freedom House con ducted a survey of 193 countries of 
the world, they listed only 90 countries as democracy; they had listed 60 countries as partly 
democratic and the rest has non democratic. India has been included in the 90 countries. But 
if the present trend, continues for some more years, of dispensing with elections at the party 
level, depending entirely on nominations, we will very soon get into the category of partly-
democratic countries. And, God knows what will happen then. The way the Parties are being 
run by individuals would really be a matter of envy for the great dictators of the world. That 
generation dictators has gone. They also called the mselves democratic and we looked at 
them with contempt; but this is the way our Parties are being run today. Certain individuals 
run the parties as it God has given them the wisdom and the right to do so and we call that 
democracy. If we continue this trend, we will not b e justified in claiming that the world 
outside will be looking to us for inspiration and our democracy will be having greater lustre 
and eminence.  
The second point connected with the future of democracy I wish to flag on this occasion 
is the devaluation of the institutions of democracy. Sir, how many minutes are given to me?  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P. J. KURIEN): Fifteen minutes.  
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER: Thank you, Sir. I don't have the time to refer to devaluation of all 
the institutions of democracy. But let me take the devaluation of the institution to which we 
all  belong, namely of the institution of legislature. Sir, among all the institutions of democracy, 
namely, legislature, executive, Civil Service, Judiciary for forces and non-political military 
service, the most important is the one in which we are members, the legislature. Can we 
honestly say, Sir, that the legislatures in our country at the central level and at the State level 
are being run in the manner in which the legislatures should be run?  
Sir, I came to this House six years ago. Looking around the Benches, I could see some of 
the brilliant parliamentarians, some very brilliant minds in this House and I always used to tell 
my friends mat the Rajya Sabha is very rich in talents. On this side and that side and in the 
back Benches of the nominated Members, we find men of outstanding talents. But do you 
give them a chance to participate in debates, to contribute to the working of democracy in 
this hallowed institution? Do we find even the most talented people being able to make their 
contribution effectively in the legislature? Do we discuss the problems which should be 
really worrying us almost day-to-day as the custodians of democracy in this country. Take 
some of these problems. Farmers are committing suicide, not in hundreds but in thousands. 
The Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme is supposed to be the star scheme and I,agree it 
has to be the star scheme for fighting poverty. The re are issues like the corruption in this 
country, the all-pervasive corruption that is eating into the vitals of our nation. Do we get the 
time to discuss any of these issues in depth ? The only debate that I can recall, which has 
been seriously conducted in this House both by the Opposition and by the Government and 
which will stand out as one of the best debates this House has witnessed in the past six years 
that I know of, was the debate on the 'Indo-US Nucl ear Cooperation.' But what about the 
other subjects which are of equal importance to us?  Why are we not spending days to 
consider them, discuss them and why are we not giving freedom to the Government Benches 
to express their views during those discussions? No voting is involved, but still a whip is  

204 Motion of Thanks  [RAJYA SABHA]  on President's Address  
indirectly given to them not to oppose Government p olicies, most unlike the working of 
democratic institutions in western countries. We really have to revise the way we, conduct our 
own business in this House. Otherwise, this institution will get devalued and become a subject of 
ridicule.  
Sir, let me raise another warning signal. The probl ems, which should be worrying us, 
causing us sleepless nights, seem to be completely forgotten and we try to build up our dreams 
and to live in a dream world of our own. We go about telling the people that in twenty years' time or 
now in twelve years' time, India is going to be one of the developed countries of the world. By 
merely making bhasans to people who are not aware of facts and figures that by 2020 India will 
join the ranks of the most developed countries of the world, we are deceiving them and we are 
deceiving ourselves. It is because as I see the situation today, most unlikely, we will — and I say 
again with full sense of confidence and with all humility— reach most unlikely the levels of the 
developed countries of the world even in a hundred years. Sir, the United Nations Development 
Programme Report is very significant. They have put us down at the 128* rank in the countries of 
the world from the point of view of human development based on income, literacy or education and 
healthcare. Our per capita income is one-tenth that of the developed countries. The UNDP Report 
says that even if the developed countries do not add one dollar to their income and remain static and 
India tries to reach that level, it will take one hundred years to reach that level. When that is the 
reality and when we have to face that problem with that reality in mind, we go on telling people 
that within 12 or 20 years from now, we are going to enter into the ranks of the developed 
countries of the world. Selling dreams is easy, Sir. You can win votes for five years but you 
cannot be doing this every fifth year because you will get into trouble. Once the disillusioned 
masses feel the winds of change and feel the winds of what is happening in the country, the 
distortions in the distribution of wealth, they are not going to keep quiet. And then our democracy 
itself would face new problems which may be dangerous for its very existence.  
I now come to strategies for development. Since the time is limited, I would refer to only the 
main strategy that should be relied upon, that is, the Rural Employment Guarantee Act. I have great 
faith in this Act; I have great faith in this scheme. Mr. Manohar Joshi was Chief Minister of 
Maharashtra when I was the Governor of the State. During the ten years that I was Governor of 
Maharashtra, the State had contributed so much to the reduction of unemployment in rural areas 
that they had practically snubbed the edge of poverty, the de-humanising poverty in certain rural 
areas of the country. The Employment Guarantee Sche me, according to the President, is 
expected to soften the sharp edges of poverty and offer basic livelihood and security. Sir, the way 
we have started does not give me any hope; if this scheme is implemented, We may spend Rs. 
20,000 crores, but the number of households helped, the number of unemployed people assisted, 
will be much less than what we have ever bargained for. I will give you one piece of statistics 
which should make us think about the direction in which this scheme has been proceeding. It has 
been seen from the report published by the Ministry that during the year 2006-2007, 2.10 crores 
of households have benefited by the Employment Guarantee Scheme. I request the House to note 
these figures carefully. According to the published report of the Ministry of Rural Development 
during the year 2006-07,2.10 crores of households have benefited from the scheme. But if you go 
deep into the report — not that report but other reports published by the same Ministry — you 
will find that, in the same year, when you claimed that 2.10 crores of households have 
benefited, actually, only 37 days was the average n umber of days when employment was 
provided. While 100 days' employment has been provided for in the Act, only 37 days of  

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   205  
average employment had been provided during this period. Where are the 100 days? Where are the 
2.10 crores of households said to have benefited by the scheme? Not only that, only 7.59 lakhs of 
households out of the 2.10 crores of benefIcary had received 100 days of employment. This is 
a dismal story. This is not the way that this scheme should have started. If we go at this rate, people 
would lose confidence in that. And, therefore, it i s time that a Parliamentary Committee is 
appointed to give a new direction to this scheme and to ensure that the hopes and aspirations of 
those who introduced this scheme are really fulfilled on proper lines on which this scheme was 
expected to be implemented.  
One simple point that I will mention as a success s tory in Maharashtra. They gave 
practically complete flexibility to the local bodies and to the local officers to decide about 
entitlement and the type of employment to be given and one direction they gave was that they 
can link the Rural Employment Scheme with Horticulture Development Scheme. It was a 
wonderful decision. The result was, Maharashtra which had hardly 173 thousand hectares of 
horticulture in 9 or 10 years, from 1990 to 2000, because of the linkage of the Employment 
Guarantee Scheme with the Horticulture Development Scheme, the number of hectares under 
employment cultivation increased from 117 thousand to 971 thousand hectares and women were 
the greatest beneficiaries. Instead of asking them to dig mud and carry heavy loads on their starved 
heads and bodies, they were doing cultivation, which they like even without assistance, of fruits 
and vegetables and they earn much more man they could. Like that, we could give direction and 
there should be some special committee of the Parliament to give direction. Otherwise, this 
ambitious scheme can go waste. Sir, I now come to the most important point that I wish to make 
and that is with regard to some of the real sad problems of our nation which seem to have escaped 
our attention and concern. We speak of poverty, but the type of poverty mat our people have is 
what Arjun Sengupta has brought out in his Report. I do not know whether he is present here. It is a 
very useful and valuable Report on the unorganised sector in our country and we got that 
astonishing figure that 79 per cent of 395 million workers in the unorganised sector are living with 
Rs.20 a day or less. To keep a cat in our house or to keep a dog in our house, we have to spend, at 
least, Rs.300 or Rs.400 a month, and here we are keeping our own workers, our own flesh and 
blood, calling them workers in the unorganised sector, and allowing them to live within Rs.18 or 
Rs.20 a day. Arjun Sengupta Report has not even been brought before this House. I wonder why it 
is not being discussed in this House. Such a Report should have got top priority over many other 
reports and should have been discussed here. But we have not done it. These are the points that 
arise from the Speech. There is my last point and that is an omission in the Speech. I do not, Sir, 
why there was no mention of it in the Speech. When all other matters have been discussed and 
when a whole catalogue of scheme has been introduced or referred to, why we—those who 
drafted the Speech—have not advised the President to say a paragraph on all pervasive corruption 
that has destroyed all development schemes as is threatening to put us back to where we were 
even 10 years earlier. Sir, to speak about corruption is to invite criticism because people say that 
they have heard the story before or they will say put your search light inside and see whether your 
civil servants are not corrupt or more corrupt than we politicians. Whatever we may say, Sir, the 
unfortunate situation today is mat civil servants, and that to senior civil servants, politicians, 
educationists, and even those who control the temples, mosques and churches are also indulging 
in corruption. And, this corruption is so prevalent that we are all tolerating it as if nothing is of 
consequence in this land of Mahatma Gandhi. It is not only a tragedy but it is a crime. The greatest 
man ever born in this  

206 Motion of Thanh  [RAJYA SABHA]  on President's Address  
world in the 20th Century, Mahatma Gandhi, is great  not because he gave us freedom, others have 
given freedom to their countries; not because he sh owed us a new way of attaining freedom, others 
have followed different course; the greatest claim for his greatness as Mahatma is cleanliness in publ ic 
life, absolute, impeccable, unquestionable integrit y. In his land, if we have descended to this level of 
corruption, no amount of praise for the development  schemes will be of any avail. Therefore, this 
has been a conspicuous omission in the speech. With  these words, I conclude my speech.

[4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   229  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN ): Shri Prasanta Chatterjee, your party is 
left with one minute only. But you should conclude in ten minutes. ...(Interruptions)... 
What is left is one minute only, but you can conclude in ten minutes. I am giving you ten 
fold increase.  
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE  (West Bengal): Sir, I will try and finish my 
speech within the allotted time itself. Yesterday, our leader Comrade Sitaram Yechury 
elaborately recorded the views of CPI(M) on the Presidential Address, and also in the 
context of the Government's claim on economic growth and foreign affairs, particularly, 
on Israel and the Palestinian peoples' rights. I will confine my views to other arenas.  
The views expressed in the speech of the hon. President appear to be one-sided as 
there is no admission of harsh realities. Many important issues affecting the common 
people have not found any place in her Address. How can we deny that every year, 
approximately, rupees one lakh crores are being accumulated as black money? Some 
reports have indicated this.  
Prosperity for the rich and affluent, and deprivations for the majority of people is the 
essence of today's exclusive growth. India's position in the Human Development Index is 
128 out of the total 177 countries while it was 126 last year. And, as per the Global Hunger 
Index, India's position is 94*.  
Sir, the entire country is reeling under unprecedented price rise of every essential 
commodity. Systematic demolition of the entire Public Distribution System has added fuel 
to the fire. The Union Government is slashing down the quota of foodgrains for P.D.S. 
meant for Kerala and West Bengal. Just before the commencement of this Budget Session, 
the Union Government opted for hiking the prices of petrol and diesel for the eighth time, 
without taking the course of lowering down the taxes on fuel. It is obvious that this price 
hike will lead to further rise of prices of all essential commodities.  
In spite of the growth of GDP to the extent of 8.5 per cent, the growth rate in the 
agricultural sector is only 2 per cent. This is a serious issue. Farmers should get agricultural 
inputs at cheaper prices and they should get remunerative prices for their products. Land 
reforms are extremely necessary. For implementation of these necessary steps, political will

enterprises which are employing less than ten units and having a capital of less than Rs. 25 lakhs.
