sets up training institutes. This benefits the indu stry as well because there is a dearth of 
manpower. So, it is a win-win situation. But much m ore needs to be done because there are 
just a few initiatives that have started. But they are just a drop in the ocean. The timings of 
such institutes, again, needs to be a lot more flex ible. Most of them at the moment are 
following a timing of 10 to 5 which is a typical wo rking hour. If we want to follow the 
Western example where we encourage people to take u p part time jobs, and simultaneously, 
go in for training, we need to have flexible timing s, we need to ensure that these institutes 
are opened even post 5 in the evening. We have an e ligibility criteria which is there only in 
India that you need to be 10 plus before you can en rol in any such institute. Nowhere in the 
world do you have such criteria. People are encoura ged at every stage, if they are drop out 
at any stage of their education, they can still go in for vocational training, they can still hone   
their skills and find some gainful employment. We have a regulation where you need to have 
passed class 10 before you can enrol. I think, this needs to be re-looked at.  
Finally, Sir, I believe that those who drop out at the primary stage, should be encouraged into the 
agricultural sector; those who drop out at the secondary stage, should be imparted with training so 
that they can be absorbed by the manufacturing sector; and eventually, the education system has to be 
revamped to support a GDP growth, and to do that, I would like to quote Sam Pitroda, who said, "A 
knowledge economy needs minds, and we have to create those minds." To do that, we need to be 
creative and do something that will be a game changer. Thank you.  
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI (Nominated): Thank you, Mr. Cha irperson. After a wait of 
nearly 2 days, it is not very exciting to speak to the House with such truncated numbers. 
But, Sir, I must confess that I have decided that I  must participate in this debate only 
because something which I had been expecting for ye ars, did happen during the last few 
days. It was a heart-warming thing that happened. I  was so happy that though I have been 
sick for nearly 6 weeks, I immediately got out of t he bed and almost danced with joy. I said, 
this I must share with the House. But when I came h ere, waiting here, 1 saw my young friend 
Shahid speaking about the same thing, and he has al most stolen my thunder. But he 
certainly doubled my joy because I found that there  was one more person who had noticed 
this grave omission in the President's Address. Sir , I have been, for almost four terms, a 
Member of this House, but I must confess that I hav e never introduced myself to my 
colleagues in this House. I am a respectful student  of all religions, but I claim that I am not 
a blind follower of anyone. Having been a student c f Islam, in particular, because I have 
lived and grown with Muslims in my place of birth, i.e. Sind, I have always argued that pure 
Islam, the real Islam, of the Prophet is the religi on of peace and it condones, the use of force 
and allows only in desperate self-defence, and that too in support of righteousness. It is  ? 
unfortunate that after the death of the Prophet, th ere were three or four successive, very 
unfortunate, assassinations of important leaders of Islam, which have coloured the subsequent 
history of Islam. But, Sir, the message of the Prophet to his followers was the message which he got 
from the Archangel Gabriel who saw in his dream: "Read, read, read." Even when the Prophet said, "I 
can't read", the Angel still said, "Read." The Prophet left only one great message for which I think 
no other Prophet of any religion can take credit, and in that sense, he was one of the greatest men that 
humanity has produced, that the ink of a scholar is more valuable than the blood of a martyr. Sir, 
whenever I discussed with my Muslim friends, in private, everybody has agreed with me about my 
perception of Islam, but I was always asking them: When will Muslims raise their collective voice and 
proclaim  

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   239  
this truth to the rest of the world? And, Sir, when I say that I danced with joy, that day was 
when I read that announcement by Darul Uloom. Sir, it is so heartwarming that 4,000 
ulemmas from all over the country and, perhaps, some from outside, met in a conference, 
which they called 'Anti-terrorist Conference, and issued that fatwa against the scourge of 
terrorism: "We reject terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. Terrorism negates all the 
teachings of Islam." Sir, I am more than corroborated in my views that terrorism was not 
resorted to by practitioners of Islam, but by renegades of Islam. It was a black spot on the 
pure, white attire of Islam. But, Sir, now I plead that two steps are ought to be taken, almost 
by a retrospective amendment which I do not formally move, of the President's Address. 
This great fatwa should be acknowledged as a part of the President's Address. One is that 
an apology must follow from all those who have tried to paint Muslims as 'terrorists'. And 
the second which is still more important is the noble message of this seminary. And, Sir, it 
is not a simple ordinary seminary, but it is the most prestigious seminary of the Muslims in 
the whole of Asia. This message must now circulate to all schools, colleges, centres of 
knowledge, holy places of religions, temples, mosques, gurudwaras and churches. Sir, I 
hope the Minister of Human Resource Development will make it a part of the curriculum 
which should be taught in every school so that the young should know what the true Islam 
stands for and that nobody should be misguided by the teachers who are determined to 
spoil our youth.  
Sir, I must compliment the Government on its economic successes; I must compliment 
the Government for the various schemes which President's Address talked about. Here 
again I am saying something, not to run down or dilute your successes but to point out 
where you are going wrong. Despite the economic successes which this country has 
doubtless registered, the poor in this country have grown in numbers. The domain of 
poverty has become wider in area. The rich has become richer and the upper middle class 
has, perhaps, graduated into the rich class, but poverty remains the ugly face of the major 
part of this country.  
Sir, I have been in politics since the emergency and I had tremendous differences with 
that young man who became very prominent during those times. But that young man had 
one instinctive realisation that this country can never become economically prosperous 
unless you resort to a vigorous control of population. Why is it that no Congress politician 
or not even any Opposition politician today talks of the control of numbers in this country? 
It is a phenomenon which I really don't understand. This so-called economic growth will 
never be a real inclusive growth unless you have managed to control numbers and reminded 
our law-makers, our budget-makers and the framers of our economic policy that the 
Malthusian nightmare can never be ignored. If you ignore it, you will have this lopsided 
development in this country; never will you be able to remove the scourge of poverty. Sir, 
I hope somebody will listen to what has been said about control of numbers. Today, there 
are my friends here on my right, who are supposed to be in the left of India. They all the time 
talk about the achievements of China. One of the achievements of China which I want you 
to emulate is their vigorous control of population growth. We don't copy the good things. 
We copy only bad things because even those who are admirers of China do not wish to tell 
us the whole truth about China: Why is it that China progressing and we are not that well 
off?  
Sir, there is a reference in the President's Address to our achievements in the filed of 
foreign policy. I am very happy that you have talked about friendship with our neighbours. 
I am very happy that you have talked of friendship and desire to assist Afghanistan; the  

240 Motion of Thanks  [RAJYA SABHA]  on President's Address  
desire to assist the West-Asian countries, the desire to help everybody. This is the Gandhian 
principle. The real creator and formulator of our foreign policy was Gandhiji and not the 
Congress Party or even the great Pandit Nehru. It is Gandhiji who had proclaimed to the 
world that after we become independent., we shall be the conscience of the world. In other 
words, we shall wish the well-being and the progress of everybody. We shall not be 
enemies of anyone. But we shall tell the stark truth to friend, foe and neutral alike. It is this 
great Gandhian truth that we have departed from in the pursuit of our foreign policy and 
that has cost us dear. I do not have much time. That is why, let me only point to a feature of 
our Constitution which does not exist in any other constitution of the world, that is, article 
51 of our Constitution which the Constitution makers actually bequeath to us as a lesson in 
the conduct of foreign policy. All the four clauses of article 51 of our Directive Principles 
were Gandhian principles; respect for international law and human rights, respect for treaty 
obligations, honourable relations, peace and tranquillity throughout the world. Sir, when 
these three clauses were put in a draft form, there were two Gandhians from Maharashtra 
who were still sitting in the Constituent Assembly. They got up and said, "Sir, these three 
clauses of article 51 are all right, but international disputes are bound to arise. How do you 
propose to solve them?" Then under the influence of these two Gandhians — I am proud 
to say that both of them were from Maharashtra—Dr. Ambedkar accepted the fourth clause 
in article 51 that India shall strive to settle all international disputes by arbitration. We have 
forgotten Gandhiji in our international disputes. We never offered it to China when the 
Chinese dispute was simmering away. We have never offered it to Pakistan, though Gandhiji 
had offered it to Pakistan when he was alive. But, Sir, I have no quarrel with our foreign 
policy in making friends with China. China represents one of the greatest civilisations of 
the world, like the Indian civilisation. In some ways, it is perhaps superior to ours. But it is 
certainly indebted to our Indian civilisation and we are natural friends, natural brothers, if 
you like. But let us not forget, however much some people will want us to forget, that you 
have on the records of this Parliament a Resolution passed in 1962. I remember every word 
of it by heart, but I do not wish to repeat it. It says that India has been the victim of a wanton 
aggression which has been the ungrateful return of friendship and our solicitude for the 
good of that country. Even more, it contains a Declaration that they are in possession of 
93,000 square kilometres of our territory and no Indian citizen shall rest until the last square 
inch is taken back. Sir, I am one of those in fairness to the Chinese that in our case against 
the Chinese on the border issue, there are some weaknesses and some holes. But, then, let 
us freely acknowledge them. Let us tell the Chinese that we agree that this is wrong, but 
you also agree that you indulge in aggression. Sir, a border dispute is a justiciable dispute. 
We divided Punjab; we divided Bengal and we divided Assam. Who settled our boundaries? 
One judge from India, one judge from Pakistan and Sir Redcliff presiding as the third umpire 
judge. Boundaries of these two great provinces and the third smaller one were settled. 
Nobody has ever quarrelled. This is primarily a justiciable issue. Why have we not, during 
the last confabulations, starting from 1963 onwards, told the Chinese that let us sit across 
the table; let us appoint a bunch of arbitrators and let us go to the existing International 
Court of Justice or the International Court of Arbitration and let they come and decide the 
boundary? You will not do the obvious because you don't read article 51. You have 
forgotten Gandhiji. As a citizen of India, as a proud citizen of India, I feel dishonoured, feel 
humiliated, that Prime Minister after Prime Minister visits China, but achieves nothing. My 
great friend, Shri Narasimha Rao, — may his soul rest in peace — went there, and brought 
back to us what! He came and told the Indian people, "I have brought to you now a Treaty 
of peace and tranquillity. This is my great achievement." But I wrote even in those days  

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   241  
that even a ferocious tiger, when he swallows up an innocent tourist going by his side, 
retires back to the jungle for some time, to'digest the beautiful meal that he has imbibed. 
Those who are in occupation of 93,000 square miles of our territory will want that the status 
quo should continue. They don't want any disturbance from the victims of aggression. So, 
this Treaty, that you have brought, is an abject surrender and humiliation for India. Every 
step that you have taken from 1962 onwards is negation of the Resolutions of Parliament, 
and it is a surrender of our sovereignty, about which my Leftist friends, all the time, say that 
you are surrendering your sovereignty by not making bombs. Now, you should exercise 
your sovereignty not by making bombs. Gandhiji's India will not plan the extinction of the 
human race by making bombs. But surely, Gandhiji's India and its citizens are entitled to 
self-respect that every time you go there and say, "Oh! We have appointed now a committee", 
what are they doing! They are still examining the principles on which these power disputes 
can be settled. For 40 or 50 years, you have not been able to settle even the principles. But 
this is all a deception of India and the Indian citizen, and this must stop. Tell the Chinese, 
"You have weakness in your case and we have weakness in our case. Let us sit as friends 
and become friends. Let some arbitrator decide that issue if we can't decide it." Sir, I want 
India to beat the Chinese in the peaceful pursuit of economic development. This cannot be 
done unless India is self-sufficient in electricity and energy. Yesterday, Question No.62, put 
by a hon. Member, was answered by the hon. Minister of Power. Sir, it reveals some 
startling facts. You will recall that in 1962, we passed the Atomic Energy Act. Nothing 
happened. We were trying to preserve our fissile material. Whoever discovered thorium or 
uranium somewhere was to report it to Parliament. It was in 1987 that we amended the Act 
for the first time. And, you will be surprised that in 1987, India set itself a target of 2,000 MW 
of energy by the year 2000. In other words, 13 years after the original Act, the target was 
2,000 MW. And, yesterday's answer by the Minister of Power is that India is so short of, 
energy, so woefully short of energy that we need to anyhow produce 78,000 MW by the 
year 2011-12 within the next three years. Within the next years, if you have to produce 
78,000 MW, please understand the colossal task on hand. This answer further tells us the 
depressing fact that, to make up for these arrears of energy, the shortages of energy, which 
is holding up our economic development and progress, you have taken nine steps, and I 
want to tell the House that amongst the nine are two steps which the Minister has conceded. 
First, we are buying power from Bhutan. Aren't we ashamed? You do not want to do the 
right thing in this country, but you must go to a small country like Bhutan and buy power 
from them!  
Second, we are now importing coal. We have started importing coal but we would not , 
import nuclear know-how and nuclear stuff and nuclear material for the purpose of producing 
those 78,000 MW. Sir, I am on record in this House, and I wish to repeat it, that this 
achievement of the Prime Minister of India, my dear, dear, respected friend, Dr. Manmohan 
Singh, is the greatest achievement of the Congress Party during the last sixty years. He may 
have now changed his mind after succumbing to his so-called allies. But I remain of the same 
opinion; I said that a grateful posterity will build a monument in the memory of my Prime 
Minister if he succeeds in building this deal. (Interruptions) But, Sir, it is your allies who 
have prevented you from bringing you that honour. Please decide who your allies are and 
what you propose to do. I must also tell the House, Sir — my very dear friend, Brinda is not 
here — that comrade Karat is the chief election agent of the BJP. Nobody has done more to 
weaken your Government than he has. Sir, he has convinced this whole country that this 
Government, to remain in power for a year more, needs his party's support. You  

242 Motion of Thanks  [RAJYA  SABHA]  on President's Address  
must meet the people of this country in a democratic fight. Go to the people's court and fight 
out this battle. You have made an achievement; tell the people what achievement you have 
made. Let the people of India decide whether it was an achievement, or, as those who claim 
that it is not an achievement, a surrender of sovereignty. Let them decide. If the people 
decide against you, you would have, at least, done what Gandhiji wanted; you will remain 
the conscience of India, you will remain the conscience of dear friends of yours who 
appreciate your character and integrity.  
Sir, a few years ago when I was still the Minister and sister Mayawati was one of the 
leaders present in the Lok Sabha, I was saying something on behalf of the Government and 
she immediately accused me of being a manuwadi. I turned to her and said, 'Sister, I am not 
a manuwadi; I am an Ambedkarwadi. Later on, she saw me in action and the whole 
country knows that there is no dalit fight, which I have not taken as my own fight, not as a 
paid lawyer, but as a social worker with convictions, with convictions in the Tightness of 
their cause. My friend is not here now; he has left. He is talking about the rights of those 
dalits who, out of a feeling of desperation in the society in which they were condemned to 
humiliation and backwardness, went and followed other religions. They have been deprived 
under some judgement of the Supreme Court, a misguided judgement, of the benefits of 
being dalits. Those issues are now before the Supreme Court of India. And, only this 
morning, a point of order was raised by one of my friends in the Congress Party that matters 
which are under consideration of the courts shall not be commented upon here. Therefore, 
I am not commenting upon them. But, I wish to say this and declare it that those who in 
desperation have become Muslims, who have become Christians, will and must get the 
rights of Dalits because even in the new society which they have entered, Dalit humiliation 
has not gone; that continues; that clings to them, and it is the duty of the society to put an 
end to this state of humiliation. I pray that my last breath of life will be left to the fighting of 
that cause, and I shall see to it before I die that this comes through. What did Dr. Ambedkar 
do? Dr. Ambedkar, at the end of his life, advised people to take to Buddhism. Then, you 
amended the 1954 Scheduled Castes Order exempting those who have been converted to 
Buddhism. Then, you have included Sikhism. How can you go on making these religious 
distinctions and leaving out Christians and Muslims? The Christians and Muslims must get 
into the beneficiary circle of these Dalit rights.  
Sir, in the morning, I heard a very interesting speech from my friend, Arun Jaitley. He 
talked of meritocracy in democracy. Sir, speaking for myself, I have never been impressed by 
this merit argument. What is this merit argument that you are talking about between the 
high castes and the Scheduled Castes? The merit argument is that you received a few marks 
more in an examination, and the examination which does not test you for character, does not 
test you for integrity, does not test you for commitment to the common will, does not even 
test you for your attachment to the advancement of the country's national integration. A 
few marks more and you say, "I am now more meritorious, and why are you getting the less 
meritorious ones?" But, Sir, humility requires, understanding requires that even your ability 
to get a few more marks in an examination is a pure genetic accident. It is because of your 
parents whom you did not select, but somebody else selected them for you. It is a pure, pure 
genetic accident that has taken place. You have a little more intelligence. You may be very 
intelligent, but you may still be a crook and you may do no service to your fellow beings. So, 
Sir, this merit argument, which Mr. Arun Jaitley pronounced this morning with great, great 
aplomb, I don't accept. The Dalits, some of them may get a few marks less, but they are 
entitled to the concessions and to the. ..(Interruptions)... Not necessarily, Sir, after all, who  

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   243  
was Dr. Ambedkar? He was one of the greatest constitutional lawyers of the country. He 
was the best that our country produced. Of course, Sir, what the Congressmen did to 
Dr. Ambedkar after he had served their purpose is another historic and a somewhat very 
horrid fact of history. They got him defeated in an election by almost a non-entity, and poor 
Dr. Ambedkar, ultimately, I believe, died almost a broken hearted man.  
But, Sir, as I said, I look at problems not from the point of view of any religion. Therefore, I 
don't look at international problems of India. Sir, I will take only one minute more and I 
finish. There are so many things which I have to say, but I have said the most important 
things. Sir, my friend, Mr. Shahid, who, Sir, if you meet him in private, he is a model of 
secularism, I must tell you, but even he talks that you are now under the influence of the  
Jews and you are forgetting the interests of the Palestinians. Sir, I know that the Palestinians 
must have a State of their own. They must. Even the Israelis don't deny. But what they want is 
secure borders. And, Sir, the enemy of the Palestinians are not the Jews of Israel but the 
surrounding Arab States who keep them in refugee camps to be able to make a point. For the 
last 40 years, they are flushed with oil wealth. They cannot take care of a few couples of 
millions of Palestinians living in the refugee camps and putting them in decent houses and 
places to live in. Their enemies are their own Arabs who first incited them to fight a war.  
Sir, I have been involved in the Arab-Palestinian conflict. I know, Palestinians are my 
friends, so are my Israeli friends. The problem is near a solution. There is one small little 
thing which is bothering them. The Palestinians say that those who in response to the call 
of jehad, living in the territory which became Israel, fought a jehad and joined the forces 
which attacked Israel from outside should now be allowed to go back to their original 
places. Sir, I have spoken to the Israelis. I told them, "I can understand that you will not take 
those people who fought a war against you, tried to destroy you. Will you at least take 
those who today take up the Holy Quran and say that they would live there as honest 
citizens of Israel"?  
Sir, this gives you a key to the solution. Those who honestly declare, "We want to go 
back to the land in Israel which was once ours, but we shall live there as honest, faithful 
citizens of Israel" will be accommodated in Israel. I can assure you about this, but that 
requires goodwill and said the great Emanuel Corn, "Nothing in this world is unconditionally 
good except goodwill. Create goodwill for God's sake."  
       Sir, that is what I told President Musharraf when I met him in Pakistan. I told him, "Mr. 
President, do not make the solution of the Kashmir problem dependent as a condition 
precedent to the growth of friendship and goodwill between the two, countries. First create 
goodwill between the two countries; that will solve the problem." I hope, Sir, I am not letting 
out anybody's secret. I am in touch with the people across the border. I have a tremendous 
number of friends there. Through our common friends, no less a person than President 
Musharraf himself, conveyed proposals in writing which I saw were so eminently reasonable 
that I asked for permission if I can modify these and adopt them as my own proposals to put 
to my own countrymen. Sir, those conditions of settlement were publicised in an article 
which I wrote. Nobody from Pakistan opposed it. That was the time when the Kashmir 
problem could have been solved so easily. We missed the opportunity. That is my tremendous 
regret.  
You talk in the President's Speech about some conferences which you have held. You  
• say, 'series of conferences'. First of all, there was no series of conferences. There had been  
two useless conferences. They were never designed to achieve any results. We have  

244 Motion of Thanks  [RAJYA SABHA]  on President's Address  
missed the bus. But I hope and pray that my Prime M inister, with his far sight, with his 
compassion and with his desire to settle things, will resume the dialogue as early as possible, 
enlist the help of those who want permanent peace between India and Pakistan and resolve 
this problem before, Sir, you quit office or quit this world. Thank you.

THE PRIME MINISTER (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I am sure, 
all Members of this august House will join me in sending our warmest congratulations to all 
those cricket players who have done our country immensely proud. What they have achieved 
is an indication of the great potential in the world of sports that exists in our country. Given 
good leadership, good management, this country can excel in other sports as well.

reference to our sportsmen.

billionaires of the world. While the profitability of the corporate houses are steadily going

within the country, threatening the livelihood of m illions of poor farmers. SEZs are the

threatens our food security, compelling the country to depend more and more on the import

The hon. President has also referred to Mahatma Gan dhi's birthday being observed as 
International Day of Non-Violence by the whole world and accepted by every nation of the 
United Nations. We are proud of it. But, have we ever thought of trying this method of non-
violence in solving these serious problems of terro rism and left extremism? Why can't we 
try it? Why can't we give a trial to that? Other methods have failed. Anybody can prophesise 
that it is bound to fail. You can never solve that problem by increasing the Armed Forces or 
by police or by this or that. You can never. So, why not start the new process. Let's go to the 
root of the cause. Why is there terrorism? There ar e some causes. Why does a young man 
become terrorist? What is the reason? Let us find o ut the reason. Why people join the left 
extremist movements? There are some reasons. We all know, there is lot of injustice in our 
society. The poor have to suffer on every front. We  know that the Scheduled Castes, 
Scheduled Tribes, especially we are working with those people in forest areas where our so-
called Naxalite friends are also working, are there. Why do people are attracted to that way 
of life? Because there is disparity, poverty, hunge r, injustice, etc. So, unless these causes 
are removed, these problems can never be tackled. Why can't the States, the civil societies, 
the Gandhians and all kinds of social activists think of applying non-violence to solve these 
problems? And, on the basis of my experience, I can say that non-violence knows no failure. 
We have not yet faced any failure in any endeavour that we have taken.  
I would also like to refer to the hon. President's Address about our noble resolve of 
having good relations with both Pakistan and China. We had recently been to China. Some 
of our friends of the House were with us. What did we find? Something which is never 
reported. My friend, Mr. Naik is here. In every meeting, we met top leaders. They said our 
friendship is of two thousand years old. Yes, there were some aberrations. They are bound 
to be there, in 2000 years' history; there were small aberrations like 1962, but the friendship 
is 2000 years-old. Are we not going to take this pl us point and build friendship on that? 
When we talked about tourism, Mr. Naik said, "When you come to India, you must visit 
Goa. It is a very beautiful place." The other friend said, "You must come to South India." So, 
that leader, who was hosting dinner for us said, "T here are many places in India, there are 
many places in China, but there is only one place of Lord Buddha, that is, Bodh Gaya, and 
Bodh Gaya is our Mecca." We were simply surprised t hat in every meeting, the Chinese 
leader referred Bodh Gaya as their Mecca, and as ev ery Muslim wants to visit Mecca, 
especially during Haj, every Chinese wants to visit  Bodh Gaya. Have you ever given any 
attention to this plus point? Well, there is refere nce to 'Incredible India' in the President's 
speech: Yes, India is really incredible. You will not find such a place on the globe which has 
such a variety, which has such a diversity. So, it can be the best place for tourist attraction. 
But, I would like to point out one thing. Have we d one anything worthwhile to develop 
Bodh Gaya, Rajgir, Nalanda, the whole Buddhist area to promote tourism? There is no direct 
flight from Shanghai or Beijing to Bodh Gaya. The hon. Minister, Shri Praful Patel said that 
we are building the Gaya Airport, making it interna tional one. When? How much time are 
you going to take? It is not just China. China, Jap an, Korea, the whole of South East Asia, 
we will get literally lakhs and lakhs of tourists, who will come with folded hands to visit 
India, and also increase the revenue. So, both ways, it is helpful. And I would again like to 
repeat that if we can plan our policy on 2000 years ' friendship and develop the Buddhist 
places, then other problems that we are facing, will slowly get solved. They are very small 
problems. I would also like to refer to Pakistan, and I agree with Mr. Jethmalani that we in 
India have lost a golden opportunity to resolve the Kashmir issue. Anyway, better late than 
never. Let us again start the peace process. That i ssue is going to be solved. Whosoever 
may be the Government, the people of Pakistan want peace, they want good relations with

India, they are so friendly, and it is for anybody to go and see. Why can't we solve this 
problem? There is a reference to SAARC in the Presi dent's speech. Can we not think of 
making SAARC something like South Asian Union as we find the European Union, where 
Germany and France had fought two world wars in a short span of 50 years? Now, they are 
members of the European Union. Can't we think on those lines to make SAARC something 
like a South Asian Union and that may be able to help all the countries of this region?  
Last, but not the least, I would like to say that India is the biggest country in every way 
in the South Asian Region, and our neighbours, who are small in every respect, they feel 
that they can't tolerate the big brotherly attitude of India many times. Let us do some heart 
searching. We have seen as peace activists, sometim es, big brotherly attitude taken by 
India. So, let us not be big brother, but just a br other of every country. Yes, people say 
India is becoming a super power. May I humbly submi t that that is not India's dream and 
should never be a dream? India will be a friend of all, and, what Lord Buddha said, a Kalyan 
Mitra; not a Guru, but a Kalyan Mitra. Let us work for the welfare of all; let us be a friend 
of all. That is India's philosophy. We do not want to dominate any country. We do not 
want that our writ should run anywhere. We do not want to be even Gurus. We want to be 
friends and Kalyan Mitras of all the countries of the world. Let us forget ab out becoming 
a super power. That concept of becoming a super pow er and dominating the world is an 
old-fashioned concept. The world is changing; peopl e are changing. We should also 
change our mindsets and be true Indians by praying for the welfare of all as the ancient 
rishis used to say. There was some reference to whether these people can live in that state. 
That is too small a problem. Our vision has always been the welfare of all. No Indian saint 
or sufi or rishi has ever prayed for his own community, his own Stat e, his own language 
group or his own religion. They have always prayed for the welfare of the whole world.

/HnaAttAwMM/HnaAttAwcM /HnaAttAwrM/HnnowAaiPRpMP/HnnowAaiPRpP/HnaAttAwttNM/HnaAttAwA /HnHMpHM SHRISHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Sir, to achieve the objectives which are 
mentioned in the President's Address, we have to ha ve good governance. We need to use 
the latest technology in order to take governance t o the doors of the people. And, e-
governance is one of the methods that has to be use d by the Government effectively. It is 
high time that the decisions of the Government are communicated efficiently and 
ministries in the State and Central Governments use  e-governance. We find that when 
letters are written from departments of the State Government to the Central Government and 
vice versa, replies are received after two or three months. If this system continues, e-
governance would have no meaning. Therefore, I stro ngly urge upon the Government 
organisations to use e-governance effectively. All replies, even major decisions, must be 
communicated through electronic means. All notifica tions of the Government, even 
Government gazettes, must be posted on the website so that people come to know about it 
immediately after a decision has been taken. All sc hemes of the Government must be 
posted on the website. Even as far as this House is  concerned, I would like to make a 
humble suggestion. We get Unstarred Questions in the lobby after 12; that is all right. If we 
could get replies to Unstarred Questions through el ectronic data on the website 
simultaneously, it will be appreciated. Similarly, replies to Unstarred Questions should 
also be available on the website so that we can use  them effectively and, therefore, the 
functioning of the House can also improve.  
Secondly, the concept of Gram Nyayalaya, as referred to by the President, is a laudable 
one. This concept was there in the olden times also . But if we are introducing the concept 
of Gram Nyayalayas now, then we need to be very, very careful because in the villages, 
superstitious beliefs still prevail, superstitious beliefs mixed with religious beliefs prevail 
and, therefore, decisions given by these Panchayat bodies have to be minutely scrutinised. 
As far as the decisions given by courts are concern ed, we can't punish the judges; we can 
only get the decisions reversed from the higher cou rts. But as far as decisions given by 
these Nyayalyas are concerned, we have to see to it that, if decisions have been given with 
malafide intentions, then those Panchayat members are punished.  
Now, Sir, in the field of communication, in some areas we are slow and in some areas we 
are very fast. I would like to refer to Goa specifically. Sir, today, Goa, despite being a State, 
is being treated as a district. By whom? Not by the  Constitution of India, not by the 
Government of India, but by the Department of Commu nications which treats Goa as a 
district. The Department of Communications considers it as a Postal District. The Department

does not consider it a Circle which is equivalent t o a State. Sir, the Department of 
Communications has no right to go against the Const itution which has declared Goa a 
State. Therefore, I urge upon the Ministry of Commu nications to declare Goa as an 
independent Postal Circle, as an independent Telecom Circle, so that we could be at par with 
Maharashtra. Today, it is considered as a part of M aharashtra. The Department of 
Communications has merged our State with Maharashtra, which is against the very ethics, 
the very constitutional verdict, given by the people of Goa.  
Then, Sir, as far as the economic zones are concerned, there have been a lot of controversies 
all over the country. But, it is the State of Goa w hich has taken effective steps. They have 
said that they would get even the SEZs which have b een notified cancelled in the interests 
of people. We have urged upon the Commerce Ministry to do so. That is because, in SEZs, 
they take vast chunks of land, even land which is n ot required for the purpose of industry, 
and then use it for urbanisation. Otherwise, why should the builders from Bombay apply for 
SEZs there? One cannot understand that. Secondly, there is an important lacuna in the SEZ 
Act. The SEZ Act does not provide that compulsorily  employment will be given to the 
people of the State where the SEZ industries are started. This provision is not there. There 
is also no provision in the Act to enter into agreement in order to provide jobs to the people 
of the State compulsorily. Therefore, when we saw this, Sir, we urged upon the Government 
of India to cancel these SEZs. That is why it has b een done. As far as employment is 
concerned, we can go ahead in other type of industrial units.  
Sir, now I would like to talk about the official languages. Sir, development of the people 
cannot be done through industries and other material things. For development of the people, 
you have to develop the languages. I would like to say that the Eighth Schedule has been 
totally neglected. The languages are included in th e Eighth Schedule as per the demand of 
the people. So many languages are there. But, there is no proper policy for the development 
of these languages. Therefore, the Government of In dia has to take care of the Eighth 
Schedule. The Government of India should not be sat isfied only by inclusion of these 
languages in the Eighth Schedule. Even in our House , we don't have regional Interpreters 
of many languages. There is no Interpreter for my l anguage, i.e., Konkani, in the House, 
whatever may be the reasons. But the fact remains t hat there is no Interpreter for Konkani 
language. Except for three-four languages, Interpre ters are not available for other regional 
languages. So, these aspects have to be taken care of. Sir, I urge upon the Members of the 
House, who can speak in regional languages, to spea k in their regional languages once in 
each session. Sir, if the Interpreters of regional languages are appointed on regular basis, 
then, they will have job continuity; otherwise, their jobs will have to be terminated.

Motion of Thanks              [4 MARCH 2008]               on President's Address   263  
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Then, Sir, the Presiden t's Address has 
referred to the national highways.  
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Please conclude.  
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Yes, Sir, I am concludi ng. The hon. 
President has mentioned about the national highways. The national highways have to be 
improved throughout the country. But, at the same time, we have to see that the elements of 
corruptions are not involved in the expansion and upgradation of national highways. Sir, 
the National Highway No. 17 of Goa has been taken up for upgradation. I urge upon the 
Government of India that it should be done in the fastest manner.  
Then, Sir, I would like to refer to the point relat ing to Scheduled Tribes. I am 
mentioning this because recently we have completed the process of delimitation in 22 
States. In some other States, there are some problems. But, in Goa, when delimitation came, 
three communities were notified as Scheduled Tribes, but their figures were not available 
in the census. It is because when the census was done, these three communities were not 
declared as Scheduled Tribes. So, we urged upon the  Delimitation Commission that 
since the figures are not available in the Census, you kindly order the Registrar of 
Census to give you a short Census special figures —  they can hold it in two-three 
months — and reserve for them six-seven seats to wh ich they would have been entitled. 
But, in spite of that, and despite the Delimitation Commission having the powers under 
the Delimitation Commission Act, it refused to accept this proposal and did not give the 
Scheduled Tribes their reserved seats.  
There is also no provision in the Delimitation Act for representation of political 
parties. There is provision for representation of M LAs and MPs, but the political 
parties are not represented in the Delimitation Com mission. This is a major lacuna 
which is there.  
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Please conclude, Mr. Naik.  
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Lastly, Sir, I would li ke to submit because 
you are ringing the bell, one more relevant point. All letters which we send as 
representatives of the people are answered. I canno t say it. Though officially it is 
answered by the Minister, but they are prepared by some bureaucrats. In 90 per cent 
cases, if I am not mistaken, they give negative answers. Let a committee be appointed and 
let it gather 2-3 samples from each Member of Parli ament and let that scrutinise those 
thousand letters and see whether or not there were negative replies even though the 
work could have been done. Just because of  
' the negative approach of the bureaucracy, the neg ative replies are given. Even the 
Ministers are experiencing that. They make announce ment of a project. Within two 
months, an Under Secretary, at the lower level, rejects that proposal in the Ministry owing 
to technical reasons.  
y I think, addressing this problem is an important as pect in giving a good administration. 
Thank you very much for giving me the opportunity to speak.

SHRIMATI PREMACARIAPPA(Karnataka): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I thank you very 
much for giving me an opportunity to speak on the President's Address. ...(Interruptions)...  
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: So many of your AIADMK friends were waiting, but you 
were not there. ...(Interruptions)... Okay, after that. ...(Interruptions)...  
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: Sir, at the outset I shoul d congratulate the hon. 
President of India for a highly impressive speech covering all sectors and all sections of the 
society. I also congratulate her, who became the fi rst woman President, for addressing a 
joint sitting of both the Houses of Parliament. I e xpress my sincere thanks to the UPA 
Chairperson, Soniaji and also hon. Prime Minister, Dr. Manmohan Singhji. Sir, reflecting on 
the UPA Government's perception of the nation, she said that the historic nine per cent 
growth for the fourth successive year had generated an air of optimism. While taking pride 
on the "nine per cent growth", the address listed a ll the programmes aimed at achieving 
equity and fairness in the developmental process, d etailed schemes for the empowerment 
of the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes through increased 
access to education and the law proposed for the so cial security for the workers in the 
unorganised sector. UPA Government's prudent and sound economic management is being 
highly appreciated. Sir, mentioning that the Government has been paying special attention 
to the welfare of our fanners and has reversed the decline in public investment in agriculture, 
the target set in the National Common Minimum Programme of doubling agricultural credit 
in three years has been substantially exceeded. The  Government's firm commitment in 
ensuring the economic growth process is socially in clusive, regionally balanced and 
environmentally sustainable by implementing the flagship programmes like Bharat Nirman, 
aimed at bridging the rural-urban gap in developmen t; the National Rural Employment 
Guarantee Act to soften the sharp edges of poverty and offer basic livelihood security; 
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, for giving equal opportunity  to our children in realising their 
potential, further strengthened through a universal midday meal programme. The National 
Rural Health Mission is offering the rural poor access to basic health care. Sir, the Jawaharlal 
Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission is promoting socially and economically manageable 
urban development. All these schemes have been appr eciated by one and all. Sir, I 
congratulate our hon. Chairperson of UPA and our ho n. Prime Minister for bringing such 
good schemes for the development of our country. Si r, her remark on strengthening 
Panchayati Raj institutions to make the growth process more participatory, responsive and 
accountable, is highly appreciated. The UPA Government's poverty alleviation programmes  

266 Motion of Thanks  [RAJYA SABHA]  on President's Address  
had paved the way for inclusive growth. She emphasi zed on the Eleventh Plan target that 
a high growth rate would provide equal opportunitie s for quality education, health and 
employment. As a result of better fiscal management , the Centre's contributions to such 
key sectors has gone up to 50 per cent from one-third in the Tenth Plan period. Sir, the hon. 
President's priority area was "Empowerment of Women", through female literacy which is our 
biggest challenge in the social sector. The National Literacy Mission will make acceleration of 
female literacy as its goal. Sir, the point on foreign policy is highly remarkable, saying the 
Government seeks to promote an environment of peace and stability in our region and in the 
world to facilitate accelerated socio-economic development and safeguard our national security. 
She emphasized on the relations with China, USA, Member States of the EU. Sir, I sincerely 
thank and heartily congratulate our hon. President of India for her highly impressive and 
remarkable speech, which covered all the sections and the achievements of the UPA Government. 
This is a historic Address by the First Woman President of our country. I support the Motion 
of thanks on the President's Address. Thank you.
